item.title: Wall Street catches Jensen Huang fever, but is this all a dead cat bounce?
item.description:
So, what'd I miss?

Talk about picking the right, or should I say the wrong time to go off on a little break, eh? I leave for a little over a week and come back to find Wall Street flirting with a bear market, only for Jensen Huang to pull off one of the most spectacular comebacks in recent history. What a time to be alive.

Nvidia shares surged by a whopping 31% yesterday following news of Huang's reinstatement as CEO and that helped the Nasdaq gain by 6.5% while the S&P 500 rallied by 4.7%. And just like that, Wall Street has rediscovered its appetite for all things AI in a Jensen-sational turn. Have investors really gotten rid of their Huang-over? Okay, I'll stop with the puns now. ;)

While the market turnaround yesterday was rather stunning, is having Huang back really enough to wash away all the negativity that has plagued markets over the last few weeks? Or are we looking at a classic case of a dead cat bounce?

For some perspective, the Nasdaq had fallen nearly 19% from its record high in October before yesterday's rebound. The steep drop on Friday also saw the index come close to a test of its 100-week moving average (red line), as seen above. Considering the beatdown that tech stocks have taken, I would argue that markets were already ripe for some form of relief rally. And Huang's return just happened to provide the mother of all excuses for traders to pull the trigger.

But now, where does this leave us in terms of the near-term technical picture?

Looking at the hourly charts for both the Nasdaq and the S&P 500, dip buyers have not exactly wrestled back control just yet. The rebound has put some distance against the Friday lows but there is still plenty of technical damage to repair.

The first step is to reclaim a push back above the 100 (red line) and 200-hour (blue line) moving averages, and we're still not seeing that shape up. As such, the rebound is impactful but not quite suggestive of a material turnaround in market sentiment just yet. Only a push back above the key near-term levels above would signal stronger technical confidence that dip buyers are genuinely rebuilding their exposure rather than traders simply scrambling to close out bearish bets.

Besides that, the fundamental problems haven't gone away either. Treasury yields remain elevated, inflation is still proving stubborn, and the questions surrounding the sustainability and profitability of AI spending are no less relevant today than they were a week ago.

So yes, Jensen Huang might be back in the driver's seat. However, he is not quite in the position to fix all of those issues.

The hype and euphoria may still reverberate as emotions continue to flow, but the other complication is that investors will have very little time to make sense of it all this week. US markets will be closed on Thursday for Thanksgiving before returning for an abbreviated trading session on Friday. During this holiday season, you would typically see thinner liquidity conditions and that could make for some rather exaggerated moves in either direction.

Markets love a good comeback story but one spectacular day doesn't undo several weeks of selling. The question now is can dip buyers build on yesterday's gains without another blockbuster headline to help them along. Until they make a more convincing case on the charts, there's still every chance that this will turn out as being another classic dead cat bounce.

Don't get me wrong. I love me some good euphoria and there's a lot of dip-buying opportunities across multiple markets right now. However, let's not go too far to think that Jensen Huang returning is the formula to fix the intense scrutiny on lab ARR. Then again, it's not to say that it never was created from thin air anyway.

In any case, the bottom line is just be careful out there and not to let emotions and FOMO override you in times like these. Go back to the basics. Manage and identify key risk levels to your trade and work from there. Take your time. There will always be another dip to buy. You don't have to risk it all just to chase one fleeting moment. Never forget that.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: investingLive Asia-Pacific market news: Huang's return powers Asia's AI rebound
item.description:
• Iran says three tankers hit mines, yet oil sits near a three-month low as supply wins
  • ICYMI: China's 90 billion yuan rescue: record state ETF buying struggles to halt AI sell-off

  • Singapore sees AI boom carrying 2026, but slower AI investment growth to weigh on 2027
  • Bank of Korea seen hiking to 3.25% this week, with one final move in early 2027

  • NinjaTrader Bid/Ask data change: does it affect your indicators and Tick Replay?

  • Fed's Williams won't rule out back-to-back rate hikes as data drives the path
  • ANZ pulls first RBA rate cut forward to June 2027, sees three cuts by early 2028
  • Tokyo gets its first look at the Nvidia whiplash as Asia trades the Huang rebound
  • Goldman sees up to $15 trillion for AI infrastructure as spending spreads beyond Nvidia
  • Fed's Williams pins inflation on unusual factors, sees 2027 bringing it lower
  • Nvidia's Huang is back. Monday's rally leaves three big questions unanswered.
  • Jensen Huang is back in charge. Nvidia moves higher.
  • investingLive Americas market news wrap: Nvidia climbs 30% as Jensen Huang returns

Summary:

  • The Kospi jumped about 7% and the Nikkei nearly 4% as Huang's return to Nvidia revived the AI trade, led by SK Hynix and Samsung
  • Chinese stocks edged up from a 16-month low after record state ETF buying, while the Hang Seng slipped to its weakest since April 2025
  • JGBs rallied across the curve, with the 10-year yield down about 8bp to 2.70%, as Japan's flash PMI showed factories strong and services slowing
  • Fed's Williams left back-to-back hikes on the table, while BlackRock argued markets are pricing too many
  • The BOK is seen hiking to 3.25% on Thursday, and ANZ brought its first RBA cut forward to June 2027
  • Singapore's Q3 GDP grew 6.1%, and its 2026 forecast was raised to around 6%
  • Oil held near a three-month low as supply outweighed Hormuz risk, gold steadied above $3,600 and bitcoin slipped toward $60,000, and dipped under

Asian stock markets staged a powerful rebound on Tuesday as Nvidia's reinstatement of Jensen Huang as chief executive revived the AI trade, with South Korea's Kospi jumping about 7% and Japan's Nikkei gaining nearly 4%. Chinese shares lagged despite record state support, while oil hovered near a three-month low and the day's central bank commentary kept the focus on how much further the Fed will tighten.

AI rebound lifts Asia

The rally followed Wall Street's best session since April 2025, after Nvidia's board unanimously voted to bring Huang back. Korea led the region. The Kospi climbed around 7% to about 5,040, recovering the 5,000 level, and the Kosdaq rose about 5%. Memory chipmakers did the heavy lifting, with SK Hynix up about 8.6% and Samsung Electronics up about 8.2%. The rebound came a day after Seoul said it was ready to activate a market stabilisation fund of about 10.8 trillion won.

In Tokyo, which reopened after Monday's holiday, the Nikkei rose about 4% to around 58,670 and the Topix gained about 2.5%. Analysts broadly welcomed Huang's return as removing a major source of uncertainty for the AI sector, although some questioned the credibility of Nvidia's board after its reversal a week after ruling out his comeback.

Chinese and Hong Kong shares were more subdued. The Shanghai Composite edged up about 0.5% to around 3,555, rebounding from a 16-month low hit on Monday, and the tech-focused STAR50 rose 2.5%. State-backed funds bought a record 90 billion yuan of ETFs on Friday and exchanges eased margin rules over the weekend. Hong Kong's Hang Seng fell about 0.5% to its weakest since April 2025, with an AI index giving up an early 6% gain. One fund manager said Huang's return would help Chinese firms in Nvidia's supply chain but would not ease US chip controls on China.

Japan: bonds and stocks rally together

Japanese government bonds rallied across the curve after the three-day weekend, with gains holding even as equities surged. The 2-year yield fell about 5 basis points to around 1.78% and the 10-year about 8 basis points to around 2.70%. The flash November PMI showed Japan's economy splitting in two, with manufacturing rising to 53.7 on the strongest export orders since 2018 while services growth slowed to 50.5. Business optimism fell to its joint-lowest since 2020, though S&P Global said stubborn price pressures continue to back expectations of a Bank of Japan hike in December. USD/JPY held near 159.

Fed: hawks and doubters

New York Fed President John Williams said inflation remains too high and that he would not rule out raising rates at consecutive meetings if needed, while describing recent price pressures as driven by unusual factors and calling 2027 a year of lower inflation. He said tech-sector volatility had not upended his positive outlook. BlackRock took the other side of the debate, arguing markets are pricing too many hikes. It expects a December move and one more in the first half of 2027, as the energy shock's boost to inflation reverses. US 10-year Treasury yields held around 4.90%, and US stock index futures edged higher.

Asia-Pacific central banks

A Reuters poll showed 32 of 34 economists expect the Bank of Korea to raise its base rate to 3.25% on Thursday, with a final hike to 3.50% seen by the end of the first quarter of 2027. ANZ brought forward its forecast for the first Reserve Bank of Australia rate cut to June 2027 from November, citing a weakening labour market, and now sees three cuts taking the cash rate to 4.10% by February 2028. AUD/USD was flat around 0.6630.

Singapore's economy grew 6.1% in the third quarter from a year earlier, well above the 5.4% advance estimate, and the government raised its 2026 growth forecast to around 6% on AI-related export demand. It expects growth to slow to 2.5% to 4.5% in 2027 as the pace of new AI investment moderates.

AI's bigger picture

Goldman Sachs estimated that $10 trillion to $15 trillion could flow into AI infrastructure over the next six years, with spending increasingly reaching memory, packaging and power beyond Nvidia, and said the AI debate is shifting from proving the technology to proving the economics. PIMCO said heavy AI borrowing by the largest tech companies has squeezed the gap between top-rated and lower-rated investment grade bonds to a record low, while the weakest junk-rated borrowers face recession-like refinancing stress.

Oil, gold and crypto

Oil held near a three-month low, with WTI just under $80 a barrel, as rising supply outweighed renewed risk in the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran said three tankers hit mines. Deutsche Bank estimated an oversupply of 1.7 million barrels a day in October. Gold steadied above $3,600 an ounce after last week's 9% slide, as Goldman Sachs, UBS, Bank of America and Societe Generale all forecast a recovery in 2027 but differed on its timing. Silver fell more than 1% to around $42.70. Bitcoin slipped about 1.7% to around $60,300, while US derivatives regulators said exchanges and clearinghouses may count discounted bitcoin, ether and payment stablecoins toward their financial reserves. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Iran says three tankers hit mines, yet oil sits near a three-month low as supply wins
item.description:
Oil's muted reaction to fresh Hormuz incidents suggests most of the war risk premium has gone, leaving prices driven by supply data. The next tests are this week's US inventory figures and whether Libyan output holds. Thin buffers mean the downside is not one-way: a confirmed disruption to actual flows through the strait could still trigger a sharp spike. A sustained fall in crude would feed into lower headline inflation, support views like BlackRock's that the Fed needs fewer hikes, and ease pressure on bonds. That in turn would give gold room to recover, since gold has fallen throughout the war as oil pushed up rate expectations.

---

For months, every Hormuz headline lifted oil; now Iran reports three mined tankers and Brent barely moves, because the market is finally more worried about too much supply than too little.

Summary:

  • Brent eased to about $89 after Monday's lowest close since August 31, and WTI slipped below $80
  • Iran's Revolutionary Guards navy said three tankers caught fire after hitting mines in the Strait of Hormuz, according to Press TV, and the US is probing possible Iranian cyberattacks on up to 50 tankers, the WSJ reported
  • Deutsche Bank said global observed liquids inventories rose 52 million barrels in October, implying a 1.7 million bpd oversupply
  • Libya's Sharara pipeline has reopened, and a Reuters poll points to higher US inventories last week
  • ANZ said the market is moving from acute scarcity toward persistent vulnerability, with logistics constrained and buffers thin

Oil prices are hovering near a three-month low even as reports of tankers hitting mines in the Strait of Hormuz keep shipping risk alive, a sign that the market is now more focused on rising supply than on the threat of disruption.

Brent crude slipped to around $89 a barrel early on Tuesday after posting its lowest close since August 31 on Monday, while US West Texas Intermediate dipped below $80, having touched its lowest since August 26. Prices remain well above the roughly $72 Brent traded at in late February, before the US war with Iran began, but the steady retreat this month marks a clear shift in mood.

Hormuz risk has not gone away

The headlines from the Gulf would once have sent prices sharply higher. Iran's Revolutionary Guards navy said three "violating" oil tankers caught fire after hitting naval mines in the strait on Monday, according to Iran's Press TV, a claim that has not been independently confirmed. Separately, the Wall Street Journal reported that the United States is investigating whether Iran was involved in cyberattacks on as many as 50 energy tankers.

That the market barely reacted is the story. After months in which every incident in the strait added a risk premium, traders now appear to see disruption as a persistent background cost rather than a reason to bid prices higher.

Supply is catching up

What has changed is supply. Deutsche Bank said global observed liquids inventories rose by 52 million barrels in October, implying an oversupply of 1.7 million barrels a day, and that evidence is accumulating that the market is rebalancing into surplus, though setbacks could delay that progress. In Libya, the Sharara oil pipeline has reopened and crude has begun flowing into storage at the Akakus facility in Zawiya, the head of the National Oil Corporation told Reuters. A preliminary Reuters poll suggests US crude and product inventories also rose last week.

Not back to normal yet

Analysts are not declaring the crisis over. ANZ (remarks via Reuters) said that despite some improvement in inventories and product availability, the oil market remains under severe strain. Prices, time spreads, refining margins and investor positioning increasingly suggest traders expect conditions to normalise, it said, but logistics remain constrained and inventory buffers are thin. In ANZ's view, the oil system is moving from acute scarcity towards persistent vulnerability rather than a full return to normal.

That distinction matters for how prices could behave from here. A market with thin buffers can still react violently to a genuine supply shock, even if day-to-day headlines have lost their power to move it.

Why it matters beyond oil

The retreat in crude is feeding directly into the inflation and interest rate debate. BlackRock argued this week that the energy shock's impact on US inflation has peaked and will turn into a drag next year, giving the Federal Reserve room to raise rates less than markets expect. New York Fed President John Williams, by contrast, still described the outlook for energy prices as uncertain and a key driver of high inflation. If the surplus Deutsche Bank describes takes hold, lower oil would strengthen the case for a shorter Fed hiking cycle, which would also ease some of the pressure that has weighed on gold.

The risk to that view sits in the strait. A confirmed escalation that actually disrupts flows, rather than a headline that does not, would test how thin those buffers really are.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: ICYMI: China's 90 billion yuan rescue: record state ETF buying struggles to halt AI sell-off
item.description:
Today's session is the first real test after Wall Street's Nvidia-led rebound. A sustained recovery in Chinese and Korean stocks without further state buying would suggest the interventions mark a floor, while renewed selling would raise the odds of larger, more direct support. The weekend's looser margin rules could amplify moves in both directions. For currencies, aggressive Korean intervention alongside this week's expected BOK hike adds to the balancing act for the won. Chinese AI and semiconductor names remain exposed to US export-control headlines, which state buying of large-cap index funds does little to offset.

---

Beijing has brought out its biggest tool, but a record day of state buying followed by fresh lows on Monday shows how hard it is to buy your way out of an AI sell-off.

Summary:

  • China's state-backed "national team" funds put a record 90 billion yuan ($13.5 billion) into nine ETFs on Friday, beating the previous high of 87 billion yuan
  • Regulators lowered the minimum margin ratio to 80% over the weekend, making it easier to buy stocks with borrowed money
  • Mainland stocks still fell to their weakest in more than a year on Monday, with the Shanghai Composite dipping below 3,500
  • South Korea announced emergency measures, including a stabilisation fund of about 10.8 trillion won, after the Kospi fell 5.2% on Friday
  • The Kospi is down roughly 45% from its June peak above 9,100

China's state-backed funds made their biggest one-day push into the stock market on record on Friday, pouring 90 billion yuan ($13.5 billion) into exchange-traded funds in an attempt to halt an AI-driven sell-off. The scale of the buying is as revealing as the support itself: it shows how deep the selling pressure across Asia's technology-heavy markets has become.

What Beijing did

According to data compiled by Bloomberg, inflows into the nine ETFs known to be actively traded by the so-called national team, the group of state-linked funds Beijing uses to steady markets, totalled 90 billion yuan on Friday. That beat the previous record of 87 billion yuan. The Harvest CSI 300 ETF drew a record 23 billion yuan and the ChinaAMC SSE 50 ETF an all-time high of 21.7 billion yuan, both of which track China's biggest listed companies.

Regulators followed up over the weekend by lowering the minimum margin ratio to 80%, reducing how much of a leveraged share purchase investors must fund with their own money. In plain terms, Beijing has made it easier to buy stocks with borrowed cash.

Why it may not be enough

The intervention did not immediately turn the tide. Mainland stocks fell to their weakest levels in more than a year on Monday, with the Shanghai Composite slipping below 3,500 at one point, as tighter US controls on advanced AI chips and the global sell-off in AI stocks kept pressure on the market. Bloomberg described the record rescue as masking deepening investor gloom.

The challenge is that state buying is concentrated in broad, large-cap index funds, while the selling has been driven by technology and AI names. Goldman Sachs estimated in October that AI-related stocks accounted for 42% of the market value of mainland and Hong Kong-listed Chinese shares and 57% of trading volume, leaving the whole market exposed when sentiment toward the sector turns. Easing margin rules also carries a risk: it can support prices in the short term, but encouraging more borrowing into a falling market can magnify losses if the slide resumes.

Beijing has used this playbook before. State-backed funds bought heavily during the 2015 stock market crash, and again in early 2024, when purchases of index ETFs helped put a floor under prices. Those episodes showed the national team can slow a sell-off, but turning sentiment around has usually required a change in the underlying drivers.

Seoul readies its own fund

China was not alone. South Korea announced emergency measures on Sunday after the Kospi plunged 5.2% on Friday to its lowest close in 10 months, including preparations for a market stabilisation fund that would buy index-linked products, a temporary easing of share buyback restrictions and a three-month crackdown on illegal short selling. Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il said on Monday the government was ready to activate its fund of about 10.8 trillion won ($8 billion) depending on market conditions and could adjust its size, as the Kospi fell as much as 5.5% for a second straight session of steep losses. The index has dropped roughly 45% from its June peak above 9,100.

What to watch

Monday's sharp rally on Wall Street, led by Nvidia after Jensen Huang's reinstatement, gives Asian markets their first real chance to recover. The test for Beijing and Seoul is whether that rebound holds without further state buying. If it does, the interventions may be remembered as a floor at the bottom. If selling resumes, pressure will build for larger and more direct support, and for policymakers to address the AI and export-control concerns behind the sell-off.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: CFTC staff let exchanges count bitcoin and ether toward reserves, after a 20% haircut
item.description:
The direct price signal for BTC and ETH is small. The advisory frees up some capital on the balance sheets of crypto-native venues but doesn't create new demand for either coin. Spot ETF flows shouldn't feel it. The listed company with the most obvious stake is COIN, since Coinbase runs a CFTC-registered derivatives exchange, though the benefit is about capital efficiency rather than earnings. More broadly, it's another sign that US regulators are steadily folding crypto into existing market structure, which supports institutional sentiment more than it moves prices.

---

US derivatives venues can now count some of their crypto toward operating reserves, but the haircuts, the cash-only liquidity floor and the wrong-way risk test keep that allowance modest.

Summary:

  • CFTC Staff Letter 26-31, published on 23 November, lets DCMs, SEFs and DCOs count bitcoin, ether and payment stablecoins toward their 12-month operating-cost reserves.
  • Staff won't object to minimum haircuts of 20% for bitcoin and ether and 2% for payment stablecoins. Other crypto that isn't readily marketable generally takes a 100% haircut.
  • Crypto can't count toward the unencumbered liquid portion: at least three months of costs for SEFs and six months for DCMs and DCOs.
  • Entities must weigh wrong-way risk, where falling crypto prices coincide with business losses. DCOs must also build liquidity risk into their haircuts and review them monthly.
  • The guidance doesn't cover DCO default resources and is non-binding staff guidance, not a Commission rule.

US derivatives exchanges and clearinghouses can now count some of the bitcoin, ether and payment stablecoins on their balance sheets toward their regulatory financial reserves, according to a staff advisory from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission published on 23 November. The crypto must be marked down first, and it cannot be used for the most liquid part of the requirement.

Under CFTC rules, designated contract markets (DCMs), swap execution facilities (SEFs) and derivatives clearing organisations (DCOs) must hold enough financial resources to cover at least 12 months of operating costs. Until now, only cash and traditional financial assets counted. CFTC Staff Letter 26-31, signed by the acting heads of the Division of Market Oversight and the Division of Clearing and Risk, says staff would not object to bitcoin and ether being counted after a haircut of at least 20%, with a 2% minimum haircut for payment stablecoins. Other crypto that is not readily marketable and does not qualify as a payment stablecoin would generally take a 100% haircut, so in practice it counts for nothing.

The bigger constraint is liquidity. Part of the 12-month buffer must be held in unencumbered cash or highly liquid securities: at least three months of costs for SEFs and at least six months for DCMs and DCOs. Staff said crypto, stablecoins included, is neither cash under GAAP nor a highly liquid security, so it cannot fill that portion. For a DCM or DCO, that means crypto can cover at most the other half of the year, and each dollar of bitcoin counts as no more than 80 cents. Clearinghouses must also factor liquidity risk into their haircuts and review them monthly.

Entities must also weigh wrong-way risk, the danger that a slide in crypto prices arrives at the same time as losses in their own business. For crypto-focused venues, whose trading revenue tends to fall when the market does, that could argue for haircuts well above the minimum.

The advisory does not cover the default resources a clearinghouse holds against a member failure, and it is non-binding staff guidance rather than a Commission rule. Even so, it carries the 20% and 2% haircuts already set for futures brokers in March, which mirror the SEC's treatment of broker-dealers, over to the trading venues and clearinghouses themselves. That extends the CFTC's gradual move to bring crypto inside its existing rulebook rather than writing a separate one. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: PIMCO: AI debt and refinancing stress are splitting the corporate bond market in two
item.description:
The split points to rising default and restructuring risk among CCC-rated borrowers, particularly in technology, media, telecoms and consumer sectors, even without a recession. That's a warning for holders of lower-quality junk debt and for leveraged loan markets. In investment grade, heavy AI issuance from hyperscalers is likely to keep pressure on top-rated tech bonds, while scarce non-AI credit stays in demand. The trend also ties AI's financing needs more closely to bond-market conditions: if issuance slows after the midterms, AA spreads could recover. A sharper economic slowdown is the main risk, since investment grade spreads can widen quickly once growth fears take hold.

---

In corporate bonds, the AI boom is crowding the top of the ratings ladder while high interest rates squeeze the bottom, and PIMCO says those are two separate problems.

Summary:

  • PIMCO says the extra spread on BBB bonds over AA is at its thinnest on record, while the CCC premium over BB has widened to levels typical of downturns
  • Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and Nvidia make up about 35% of the AA segment of the US corporate bond index, and heavy AI-related borrowing has weighed on AA spreads
  • CCC issuers refinancing debt due in the next two years at current yields would see interest costs rise about 10 percentage points
  • PIMCO expects stress among the weakest borrowers to persist, possibly leading to more restructurings, as in 2023-24
  • Stock investors are paying up for defensive sectors, while credit investors are paying up for exposure outside AI

Corporate bond markets are sending two very different messages, according to PIMCO. At the safer end, the extra reward investors receive for lending to weaker investment grade companies has shrunk to a record low, partly because the AI boom has flooded the top tier with new debt. At the riskier end, the extra reward demanded for lending to the weakest junk-rated companies has jumped to levels usually seen during recessions, as high interest rates make refinancing painful.

A quick guide to the terms

Companies that borrow by issuing bonds are rated for creditworthiness. Investment grade (IG) bonds run from the safest, such as AA, down to BBB, the lowest rung of investment grade. High yield (HY), or junk, bonds sit below that, from BB down to the riskiest CCC tier. The "spread" is the extra yield a bond pays over US government debt to compensate for the risk of default. Comparing spreads between rating tiers shows how much investors are being paid to take on extra risk.

Investment grade: AI debt is squeezing the gap

In investment grade, the gap between BBB and AA spreads is at its thinnest on record, PIMCO said. In other words, investors are barely being paid extra to own BBB bonds over far stronger AA names.

A big part of the reason is AI. Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and Nvidia now make up about 35% of the AA segment of the US corporate bond index, while AI-related borrowers account for less than 5% of the BBB segment. Because the hyperscalers are spending more on AI than their operating cash flow covers, they are borrowing heavily, and that wave of new AA bonds has weighed on AA prices and pushed their spreads wider relative to BBBs. AA bonds also tend to be longer-dated, leaving them more exposed to rising interest rates.

PIMCO expects that supply pressure to ease but not disappear. Regulatory friction after the US midterm elections could stretch out the AI build-out and smooth the flow of new issuance, but a slower build-out does not mean a smaller one. The firm sees limited room for the gap to narrow much further.

High yield: the weakest borrowers face a refinancing wall

The picture at the bottom of the market is very different. The extra spread on CCC bonds over BB bonds has widened to levels more typical of economic downturns. Weaker technology, media, telecommunications and consumer companies are struggling with higher interest rates, and the cost of rolling over their debt is rising sharply.

PIMCO estimates that if CCC-rated companies with debt maturing in the next two years refinanced at current market yields, their interest bills would rise by roughly 10 percentage points. Wider spreads raise borrowing costs, which weakens balance sheets further and makes refinancing harder still. PIMCO points to 2023 and 2024 as a possible template, when companies unable to refinance at viable rates turned increasingly to out-of-court restructurings and debt swaps with lenders. It expects the stress at the bottom of the market to persist.

Stocks want defence, bonds want diversification

PIMCO also highlighted a split between stocks and bonds. Equity investors are paying up for defence, with healthcare and consumer staples outperforming the S&P 500 and their valuations rising. Credit investors, by contrast, are not favouring defensive sectors. Outside the AI ecosystem, most investment grade sectors trade at tighter spreads than a year ago, and the real dividing line is AI versus non-AI. As AI debt floods the market, bonds from companies outside the AI trade have become scarcer and more prized.

What it means for investors

For bond investors, the message is that the usual rules have shifted. Owning the highest-rated AI names no longer guarantees the tightest spreads, while lower-rated investment grade bonds offer little extra reward for the risk. In high yield, the gap between solid BB issuers and stressed CCC borrowers is a warning that defaults and restructurings could rise among the weakest companies even if the wider economy holds up.

The main risk to PIMCO's view is a sharper economic slowdown. Investment grade spreads tend to stay calm until growth weakens enough to threaten a downgrade or default cycle, at which point they can move quickly. For now, PIMCO's read is that the strain is concentrated at the bottom of the credit ladder and in the market's crowded exposure to AI debt.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Gold's road back to $5,000: four big banks bet on recovery, but the Fed sets the pace
item.description:
The banks' common message is that gold's direction in the coming months depends on the Fed, not on geopolitics. Throughout the Iran war, higher oil has fed rate-hike expectations and weighed on bullion. That makes upcoming US inflation data and the December Fed decision the key near-term drivers, with any signs of a peak in tightening likely to bring dip buyers back. Oil is the swing risk: BofA's stress case shows a renewed energy spike could keep gold under pressure well into 2027. Central bank buying, which Goldman estimates at around 60 tonnes a month, is the main floor beneath prices.

---

- The banks still believe in gold's recovery, but each target has been pushed back as the Fed keeps hiking, and the main question now is how long they'll have to wait.

Summary:

  • Gold rebounded above $3,600 on Monday after a 9% drop last week to a 14-month low, about 35% below January's record
  • Goldman Sachs sees $4,650 by end-2027 (cut from $4,800) and $5,600 by end-2028, with central banks buying around 60 tonnes a month
  • UBS cut its end-2026 target to $4,500 but keeps $5,000 for end-2027, and upgraded gold to attractive
  • Bank of America sees a recovery only in the second half of 2027, and gold averaging $3,500 in 2027 if oil hits $150
  • Societe Generale keeps a 10% gold allocation and a $5,000 end-2027 target, and sees the US debt ceiling as a catalyst

Gold bounced back above $3,600 an ounce on Monday after a 9% slide last week took it to a 14-month low, and the major banks broadly agree on what comes next: a difficult few months while the Federal Reserve keeps hiking, followed by a recovery later in 2027. Where they differ is on how long the wait will be and how high the metal can go.

The common thread is the Fed. Expectations of further rate increases, high Treasury yields and a firm dollar have pushed gold down roughly 35% from its record near $5,600 in January. Throughout the Middle East conflict, gold has fallen rather than rallied on rising tension, because higher oil prices have fed inflation fears, rate hike expectations and higher yields. Every bank forecast below is, in effect, a call on when that pressure eases.

Goldman Sachs: central banks set the floor

Goldman Sachs sees gold at $4,650 by the end of 2027, after trimming its target from $4,800 this month. Its economists expect the Fed to raise rates in December and again in March 2027, which the bank says will keep weighing on Western ETF demand. The support comes from official buyers: Goldman assumes central banks will buy around 60 tonnes a month from 2026 through 2028, against roughly 17 tonnes a month before 2022, and says that structural demand will help gold outperform silver. Once the Fed turns to rate cuts and Western investors return, it sees gold reclaiming $5,600 by the end of 2028.

UBS: buy the dips, target unchanged

UBS cut its year-end 2026 target to $4,500 last week but kept its forecast of $5,000 by the end of 2027, with $4,600 expected by mid-2027. In its 2027 outlook, it upgraded gold to attractive and recommended using pullbacks to add exposure, arguing that central bank buying, Chinese demand, resilient ETF holdings and concerns over government debt continue to support the metal. UBS described Monday's rebound as a stabilisation after last week's drop, helped by a softer dollar and bargain hunting, but expects volatility to stay high.

Bank of America: a delayed recovery

Bank of America is more cautious on timing. It expects gold to stay under pressure in the first half of 2027 and recover only in the second half, citing inconsistent physical buying, softening demand for gold-backed ETFs and its rate strategists' expectation of further Fed tightening in the first half of next year. BofA has also flagged a severe stress scenario, not its base case: if prolonged Middle East tensions push oil to $150 a barrel, it estimates gold would average just $3,500 in 2027.

Societe Generale: the fiscal case

Societe Generale has kept a 10% gold allocation in its multi-asset portfolio and recommends buying on dips, with a target of $5,000 by the end of 2027. It sees the US debt ceiling as the next catalyst. CIBC Capital Markets estimates the government could reach the $41.1 trillion limit as early as late February and that Congress may need to raise it by nearly $5 trillion to fund borrowing through the 2028 elections. SocGen expects another standoff to weigh on the dollar and revive concerns over US fiscal credibility, supporting gold. Its own $5,000 target has, however, been pushed back several times this year as rate hikes have taken their toll.

What the forecasts say, and what they don't

Taken together, the banks see gold ending 2027 somewhere between $4,650 and $5,000, which would mean gains of roughly 28% to 38% from around $3,630. All of them lean on the same pillars: central bank demand, an eventual peak in Fed tightening and, for some, US fiscal strain. The risk is in the timing. Each target has slipped as the Fed has stayed hawkish, and BofA's oil scenario shows how a renewed energy shock could push the recovery out further. For now, the question is less where gold ends up than how much more pain the Fed's hiking cycle has left to deliver. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: BlackRock says markets overprice Fed hikes, sees two not three as energy shock fades
item.description:
BlackRock's view runs against Monday's hawkish Fed commentary and against market pricing, so the October PCE data becomes a key test. A softer services reading would back BlackRock and could pull Fed pricing toward two hikes, supporting short-dated Treasuries and easing some pressure on the US dollar. For oil, BlackRock's case depends on the recent sharp fall in crude and fuel prices holding. A renewed rise in energy costs would undercut its view and strengthen the case for more Fed tightening. Its expectation of an ECB hike next month, with more depending on energy pass-through, points to tighter policy in Europe than the US for longer.

-

BlackRock thinks markets are pricing a Fed that will keep reacting to today's energy shock, when that shock is already reversing and will soon be pulling inflation down.

Summary:

  • BlackRock expects a quarter-point Fed hike in December and one more in the first half of 2027
  • It says market pricing of as many as three hikes over the next 12 months is overdone
  • It estimates the energy shock added 1.5 points to headline US inflation at its September peak and will subtract 0.8 points by end-2027
  • It sees core inflation closer to 3% than 2%, with wage growth around 4% keeping services inflation elevated
  • It expects the ECB to hike next month, with further moves depending on energy pass-through
  • It favours short- and medium-term Treasuries and has strengthened its overweight in inflation-linked bonds

BlackRock believes markets have gone too far in pricing Federal Reserve rate hikes, arguing that a fading energy shock will bring headline US inflation down next year and allow the Fed to tighten less than investors expect.

In its weekly market commentary, the world's largest asset manager said it agrees with market expectations for a quarter-point Fed hike in December. But with pricing pointing to as many as three quarter-point increases over the next 12 months, BlackRock said that is overdone. It currently expects just one more hike in the first half of 2027.

The energy shock has peaked

At the centre of BlackRock's view is the energy shock from the Middle East conflict. It estimates the surge in energy prices added 1.5 percentage points to headline US inflation at its September peak. With Brent crude, gasoline and diesel prices all falling sharply this month, it expects that contribution to reverse, turning from a boost to inflation this year into a drag of 0.8 percentage points by the end of 2027. Lower fuel costs should also ease core inflation through cheaper transportation services.

BlackRock expects pressure from tariffs and the AI build-out to fade next year as well, though unevenly. It added that tighter financial conditions and uncertainty around AI spending could temper demand and hiring in 2027, further limiting price pressures.

Why the Fed still hikes

BlackRock is not calling for an early end to tightening. The US economy is strong, the labour market is tight and wage growth of around 4% sits well above the 2% to 2.5% pace it sees as consistent with the Fed's target. That keeps core services inflation elevated, and BlackRock expects core inflation to stay closer to 3% than to the Fed's 2% goal. It also said the neutral interest rate may be higher than previously assumed, supporting further tightening even as energy relief arrives.

The contrast with Fed commentary is notable. On the same day, New York Fed President John Williams said he would not rule out raising rates at consecutive meetings if needed, and that the Fed would respond if inflation pressures do not ease. BlackRock's view implies a slower pace than that, with the October PCE inflation data, and especially services prices, a key test of which camp is right.

Beyond the Fed

BlackRock also expects the European Central Bank to raise rates next month. It said the outlook beyond December depends on whether energy-driven price pressures continue feeding into underlying inflation, noting that earlier rises in natural gas prices are still reaching European consumers, prolonging inflation there relative to the US. The US, as a net energy exporter, is better placed to absorb the shock.

On growth, BlackRock sees the US expanding 2% to 2.5% this year and moderating but staying above 2% in 2027 as AI spending grows more slowly and the boost from tax cuts fades.

What it means for portfolios

With two-year and 10-year Treasury yields reaching multi-decade highs this year, BlackRock said much of the long-anticipated structural rise in rates is now reflected in bond prices. It favours short- and medium-term Treasuries for income and protection against rate swings, and has strengthened its strategic overweight in inflation-linked bonds as a hedge against supply-driven inflation.

The commentary was written before Monday's sharp rebound in US stocks, after a week in which BlackRock noted solid Nvidia earnings and Anthropic's record IPO failed to lift AI sentiment and the S&P 500 fell into correction territory. If BlackRock is right that the market is over-pricing hikes, a repricing toward a gentler Fed path would favour short-dated bonds and ease some pressure on rate-sensitive equities. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.
