item.title: Analysts cheer Huang's Nvidia return but question the board's sudden U-turn
item.description:
For investors, the reaction splits into two trades: relief that Nvidia's strategy and customer relationships stay intact, and a new governance discount tied to the board's credibility. The valuation argument, with shares at around 11 times forward earnings according to one fund manager, gives the rebound fundamental support beyond sentiment. Political risk is now a bigger factor in AI stocks after the midterm results, with regulation and limits on data centre development seen as the main threats to the infrastructure build-out. Any board changes or developments in the ongoing investigations could quickly test Monday's rally.

---

Earlier:

  • Jensen Huang is back in charge. Nvidia moves higher.
  • Nvidia's Huang is back. Monday's rally leaves three big questions unanswered.

And:

  • Goldman sees up to $15 trillion for AI infrastructure as spending spreads beyond Nvidia

---

Investors got back the CEO they wanted, but in reversing itself within a week, Nvidia's board may have swapped one credibility problem for another.

Summary:

  • Investment managers call Huang's reinstatement the most important AI-trade development in weeks, removing a major source of uncertainty
  • One fund manager says the shares remain undervalued at around 11 times forward earnings, and that the investment case never rested on one person
  • Other analysts say the board's reversal, a week after ruling out Huang's return on the earnings call, raises questions about its judgement and could lead to board changes
  • President Trump had pressed for Huang's return, and the board cited US government input on national security
  • Analysts say Huang's leadership will be key to navigating tighter AI regulation risks after the midterms, plus the ongoing investigations

Investment managers broadly welcomed Nvidia's decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as chief executive, describing it as the most important development for the AI trade in weeks. But some analysts warned that the board's sudden reversal has raised fresh questions about its own judgement.

Huang stepped down earlier this month after reports linked him to a suspected Chinese intelligence effort, and he was also accused of an affair with an Nvidia executive. Nvidia's board voted unanimously to bring him back on Monday, saying he was the right person to lead the company and that his return was in the best interests of stockholders, employees, partners and customers. Nvidia shares surged about 31% on the day, helping lift the Nasdaq Composite 6.5% and the S&P 500 4.7%, their best sessions since April 2025. In a note, Huang thanked the board and interim leadership and said he could not "wait to get back to work."

Uncertainty removed

For the more upbeat camp, the return removes a major source of doubt hanging over Nvidia and the wider AI industry. One fund manager described Huang as the visionary and architect behind the company's success, arguing that his return reassures investors that Nvidia can avoid the shift in strategy a leadership change might have brought. Huang's deep relationships with customers and suppliers, and his central role in shaping and financing the AI ecosystem, were cited as reasons his presence matters beyond Nvidia itself.

The same fund manager stressed, however, that the investment case never rested on one person. Even while leadership was in doubt, Nvidia remained an established business with proven technology, substantial earnings and a dominant market position. On that view, the shares still look undervalued at around 11 times forward earnings, with strong growth prospects.

A board under scrutiny

Other analysts were more critical of how the board handled the episode. They noted that on the company's earnings call last week, the board explicitly ruled out Huang's return. After that call, and with Arm's chief executive extending his contract there, it became increasingly clear to them that there was no credible alternative to lead the company Huang co-founded. One analyst said the dramatic reversal raises serious questions about the board's judgement and credibility, and would not be surprised to see changes in its make-up over time. In that view, overwhelming support from shareholders, employees and the wider technology industry was instrumental in bringing Huang back.

The politics around the decision add another layer. President Donald Trump had pressed for Huang's reinstatement, and the board cited input from senior US government officials in concluding that his return poses no national security risk. That highlights how Nvidia, a for-profit company, sits at the centre of the debate over how far US technology should be allowed to flow to countries such as China.

The bigger picture for AI

Analysts also framed the decision against a difficult backdrop for AI stocks. The sector had sold off after Democratic victories in the US midterm elections, amid concerns that new legislators could push for tighter AI regulation and restrictions on data centre development, slowing the infrastructure build-out. One analyst argued that Huang's leadership will be crucial in navigating that regulatory and political environment, as well as the ongoing investigations, and said his return could be an important catalyst for restoring investor confidence after the sharp correction.

The countercase is that the issues behind the sell-off have not gone away. Regulatory pressure, scrutiny in Washington and questions over AI spending all remain, and the board's credibility may now face closer examination from investors. Huang's return settles who leads Nvidia, but not every question about the environment it operates in.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Singapore sees AI boom carrying 2026, but slower AI investment growth to weigh on 2027
item.description:
Coming from one of the region's biggest AI winners, the comments are an early official signal that growth in AI capital spending may peak in 2026. That matters for chip and electronics supply chains across Taiwan, Korea and Japan. Markets are likely to read it as a slowdown in the rate of growth rather than a contraction, so there's limited near-term risk for AI-linked equities. Still, it adds to the debate over 2027 earnings expectations for the sector. For the Singapore dollar, firm near-term growth supports the MAS keeping its current settings in January, while the softer 2027 outlook limits the case for any further tightening.

---

Singapore's message is that the AI boom isn't ending, it's just growing more slowly, and for an economy this exposed to it, that alone is enough to roughly halve growth next year.

Summary:

  • Singapore's GDP growth outlook for the rest of 2026 remains firm, says Beh Swan Gin, permanent secretary at the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry
  • He says strong momentum in global AI investment is expected to continue for the rest of the year
  • He expects the pace of growth in new AI investment to moderate from its 2026 high
  • He says growth in most key trading partners, including the US and China, is expected to moderate in 2027
  • The government expects growth of around 6% in 2026, slowing to 2.5% to 4.5% in 2027

Singapore's growth outlook for the rest of 2026 remains firm, with strong momentum in global AI investment set to continue through the end of the year, a senior trade ministry official said on Tuesday. But he also explained why the government expects growth to slow sharply in 2027: the pace of new AI investment is set to ease from this year's high, and growth in most of Singapore's key trading partners is expected to moderate.

Beh Swan Gin, permanent secretary at the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry, made the comments after the government released stronger-than-expected third-quarter figures. The economy grew 6.1% from a year earlier in the July to September period, well above the 5.4% advance estimate, and the ministry raised its 2026 growth forecast to around 6% from a range of 4.5% to 5.5%. For 2027, it expects growth of only 2.5% to 4.5%.

Beh's remarks fill in the reasoning behind that gap. He said growth in most key trading partners, including the United States and China, is expected to moderate next year, which would weigh on demand for a trade-dependent economy like Singapore. At the same time, he expects the pace of growth in new AI investment to ease from its 2026 high.

That distinction matters. Slower growth in AI investment is not the same as a fall. Spending can stay at very high levels while still adding less to growth each year, simply because it is rising from a much bigger base. For Singapore, whose electronics exporters have been among the biggest winners from the AI build-out, even a moderation in the rate of increase is enough to pull headline growth down. Enterprise Singapore's forecasts point the same way, with non-oil domestic exports expected to jump 30% to 32% this year before slowing to 5% to 7% growth in 2027.

The comments echo concerns elsewhere in the region. In Japan, business optimism in S&P Global's November flash PMI survey fell to its joint-lowest since 2020, with firms citing worries about a slowdown in AI-related investment among their concerns. Global banks have taken a broader view; Goldman Sachs recently estimated that $10 trillion to $15 trillion could flow into AI infrastructure over the next six years, with spending spreading across memory, packaging and power.

For now, the near-term picture for Singapore looks solid. The question for 2027 is whether AI spending slows gradually, as officials expect, or more abruptly, which would hit the city-state's export engine harder. The Monetary Authority of Singapore's January policy review will be the next chance to see how policymakers weigh strong current growth against a softer outlook.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Bank of Korea seen hiking to 3.25% this week, with one final move in early 2027
item.description:
With a hike fully priced, the reaction on Thursday will depend on the BOK's guidance. A signal that the next move is the last would support the 3.50% peak view and could weigh lightly on the won, while an open-ended tone would push Korean bond yields higher. The won's 7% gain this year gives the BOK room to stay measured, but a run of Fed hikes would test that. Korean equities, already at 10-month lows after last week's tech sell-off, face the double hit of higher borrowing costs and fragile sentiment, though the semiconductor export story remains supportive for chipmakers.

---

Korea's chip boom is forcing the BOK's hand this week, but a fragile stock market and softening consumers suggest the hiking cycle is close to its end.

Summary:

  • 32 of 34 economists in a Reuters poll expect the BOK to raise its base rate by 25bp to 3.25% on November 26
  • 18 of 28 see a final hike to 3.50% by the end of Q1 2027, followed by a hold for the rest of the year
  • Inflation eased to 2.8% in October but remains above the 2% target, and semiconductor exports nearly tripled in the first three quarters
  • Weakening domestic demand and a Kospi slide to a 10-month low are expected to limit further tightening
  • The won is up about 7% this year, but a widening gap with US rates could add pressure for more hikes

The Bank of Korea is expected to raise interest rates on Thursday and follow up with one final increase early next year, according to a Reuters poll of economists, as a semiconductor-driven export boom keeps growth strong and inflation above target.

All but two of 34 economists surveyed between November 17 and 23 expect the central bank to lift its base rate by 25 basis points to 3.25% at its November 26 meeting. The remaining two forecast no change. The BOK has already raised rates by a total of 50 basis points in the current cycle. Looking further ahead, 18 of 28 economists see the base rate at 3.50% by the end of the first quarter of 2027, and the poll median shows the bank holding at that level for the rest of next year.

Why a hike looks locked in

The case for tightening rests on strong growth and sticky prices. Consumer inflation eased to 2.8% in October from 2.9% in September but stayed above the BOK's 2% target. Semiconductor exports nearly tripled in the first three quarters of the year from a year earlier, and third-quarter GDP came in much stronger than expected. Rising home prices add to the pressure.

An economist at Societe Generale said a hike is fully priced in by markets, so a decision to hold would come as a surprise. With inflation not expected to return to 2% until the second half of 2027, and with house prices still rising and chip exports robust, she said the case for another hike remains intact.

Why the cycle may end soon

Economists also see limits to how far the BOK can go. Domestic demand is weakening, and the Kospi fell to a 10-month low last week in a sharp technology sell-off, raising concerns that a hit to household wealth could weigh on consumer spending. That reinforces expectations that next quarter's move will be the last.

The currency is another factor. The won has gained about 7% so far this year, making it one of Asia's best-performing currencies, which reduces any need for the BOK to raise rates simply to support it. A separate Reuters poll earlier this month forecast the won strengthening a further 2.2% to around 1,320 per dollar by the end of April 2027.

The Fed factor

US policy could still push the BOK further. The Federal Reserve is expected to raise rates again in December, according to a separate Reuters poll, and a wider gap between Korean and US rates could weigh on the won and encourage capital outflows. One economist warned that if the BOK holds off while the Fed hikes, the reaction in currency markets would be hard to predict.

That link matters because Korea's base rate already sits well below the Fed's 3.75% to 4.00% range. By moving alongside the Fed this week, the BOK would stop that gap from widening further. If the Fed delivers more than one hike, a possibility New York Fed President John Williams left open on Monday when he said he would not rule out moves at consecutive meetings, pressure on Seoul to match it in early 2027 would grow.

The decision on Thursday will be judged as much on the BOK's guidance as on the hike itself. Any signal that the bank sees the next move as its last would support the market view of a 3.50% peak, while a more open-ended tone could revive talk of a higher terminal rate.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6757 – Reuters estimate
item.description:
The People’s Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day’s closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected CNY midpoint is typically read as a sign the PBOC is leaning against depreciation pressure, while a weaker fixing for the CNY can indicate tolerance for a softer currency, often in response to dollar strength or domestic economic headwinds.In periods of heightened global volatility, such as shifts in US rate expectations, trade tensions or capital flow pressures, the fixing takes on added significance. For investors, it provides insight into Beijing’s currency priorities, balancing competitiveness, capital stability and financial market confidence.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: NinjaTrader Bid/Ask data change: does it affect your indicators and Tick Replay?
item.description:
Well, I got this from NT.

Once my heart rate subsided (What does this mean???) I investigated. In a nutshell, NinjaTrader is cutting a data series hardly anyone uses but that clogged its servers, and the bid/ask stamp that order flow traders depend on stays exactly where it is.

Summary:

  • NinjaTrader's historical data servers will no longer provide separate historical Bid and Ask data series
  • The company says fewer than 1% of users load them, but recording them made up most of its historical server load
  • Charts, indicators and strategies built on Last price are unaffected
  • Tick Replay and order flow tools still work, because each historical trade keeps the bid and ask at the moment it happened
  • Scripts that add a standalone Bid or Ask series via AddDataSeries will lose their historical backfill and need checking
  • If a data source has no bid/ask on its trades, NinjaTrader substitutes values, so order flow readings on that data won't be accurate

NinjaTrader is retiring the separate historical Bid and Ask data series from its historical data servers, but most traders, including those who rely on Tick Replay and order flow tools, should see no change. Charts, indicators and strategies built on Last price will work exactly as before. The one group that needs to check its setup is anyone whose charts or code load a standalone Bid or Ask series to build history.

What exactly is NinjaTrader changing?

In an announcement to platform users, NinjaTrader said its Historical Data Servers will no longer provide separate historical Bid and Ask data series, as part of a push to improve the speed and reliability of historical data. The company said fewer than 1% of users load those series, yet recording them accounted for the majority of the load on its historical data servers. Retiring them, it said, allows faster and more dependable historical data for everyone. Users on the NinjaTrader community forum linked the change to a new platform release that lists historical data among its fixes.

In practice, the separate series are what a trader gets by setting a chart's Data Series to "Price based on: Bid" or "Ask", or what a developer requests by adding a series with AddDataSeries using MarketDataType.Bid or MarketDataType.Ask. After the change, those series will no longer backfill from NinjaTrader's servers.

Will Tick Replay and order flow tools still work?

Yes. The key detail is that historical tick data is still stamped with the bid and ask at the moment each trade happened. That stamp is what Tick Replay relies on. When a chart replays history tick by tick, each Last trade carries the prevailing bid and ask, which is how delta, footprint and volume profile tools classify a trade as buying at the ask or selling at the bid. NinjaTrader said Order Flow+ and similar tools are unchanged for exactly this reason.

Tick Replay never drew on the separate Bid and Ask series in the first place. NinjaTrader's own documentation notes that events from the historical bid/ask series fire only in real time in OnMarketData, which is why order flow indicators work from the bid and ask attached to each trade instead.

One caveat is worth knowing. If a data source has no bid and ask attached to its historical trades, NinjaTrader fills in substitute values, setting the bid equal to the trade price and the ask one tick higher. Order flow readings built on that data will not be accurate, so traders should confirm their data feed supplies genuine bid/ask stamps.

Who could be affected?

The traders who need to act are those who chart Bid or Ask prices directly, common among forex and CFD users, and anyone running custom or third-party code that adds a separate Bid or Ask series to load history. Such an indicator would still work in real time but would have nothing to backfill, so its historical values could be blank or misleading.

How can I check whether my indicators use the retired series?

Developers can search their NinjaScript Indicators and Strategies folders, including subfolders, for MarketDataType.Bid and MarketDataType.Ask. If those terms appear only inside checks within OnMarketData, the code is using live data and is fine. If one appears inside an AddDataSeries call, that script depends on the retired series and needs a closer look. Traders using third-party indicators should ask the vendor directly.

What if I still need historical Bid or Ask data?

The change applies to history delivered by NinjaTrader's own servers. Some broker and data-feed connections supply their own history, and NinjaTrader can record live market data locally for later use as history, which may cover traders who need a Bid or Ask series going forward. Third-party historical data vendors are another route. For the large majority working from Last price and Tick Replay, the practical effect should simply be faster historical data.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Singapore Q3 GDP jumps 6.1%, growth forecast lifted to around 6% as exports boom
item.description:
The upgrade supports the Singapore dollar and reduces any pressure on the Monetary Authority of Singapore to ease at its January review, since stronger growth argues for keeping current settings. For the region, the 30%-32% NODX forecast is a strong signal of continued AI-related electronics demand. That's positive for chip and electronics supply chains in Taiwan, Korea and Malaysia, and it comes the morning after the Nvidia-led rebound in tech stocks. The 2027 range of 2.5% to 4.5% is a reminder that the boom is expected to fade. New US licensing rules on advanced AI chip shipments through Singapore are a risk to watch for the trade hub.

---

Preview of this:

  • Economic and event calendar in Asia Tuesday, November 24, 2026: Singapore and Japan

--- Singapore's AI-fuelled export boom is even stronger than first thought, enough to lift 2026 growth to around 6%, but officials already see it fading sharply in 2027.

Summary:

  • Singapore's Q3 GDP grew 6.1% y/y, above the 5.4% advance estimate and the 5.6% Reuters poll forecast
  • Quarterly growth was 1.5% seasonally adjusted, up from the 1.1% advance reading and ahead of the roughly 1.3% expected
  • The Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry raised its 2026 forecast to around 6.0% from 4.5%-5.5%, citing an improved external demand outlook
  • It forecasts 2027 growth of 2.5% to 4.5%
  • Enterprise Singapore raised its 2026 NODX forecast to growth of 30%-32%, with 5%-7% expected in 2027

Singapore's economy grew much faster than first estimated in the third quarter, and the government responded by sharply raising its 2026 growth forecast to around 6%, underlining how strongly the city-state is riding global demand for AI-related electronics.

Gross domestic product expanded 6.1% from a year earlier in the July to September quarter, well above the advance estimate of 5.4% and beating the 5.6% expected by economists in a Reuters poll. On a seasonally adjusted quarter-on-quarter basis, the economy grew 1.5%, up from the advance reading of 1.1% and ahead of forecasts of around 1.3%. That leaves third-quarter momentum matching the second quarter's revised 1.5% pace rather than slowing, as the early data had suggested.

The Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry, renamed from the Ministry of Trade and Industry in October, lifted its 2026 growth forecast to around 6.0% from a previous range of 4.5% to 5.5%. It said the external demand outlook for the year has improved since its August assessment. For 2027, the ministry expects growth to slow to a range of 2.5% to 4.5%.

Trade figures tell a similar story. Enterprise Singapore raised its 2026 forecast for non-oil domestic exports, known as NODX, to growth of 30% to 32%, a striking pace for a key export gauge. It expects NODX growth to ease to 5% to 7% in 2027.

The advance estimate showed growth led by manufacturing, particularly the electronics, precision engineering, transport engineering and general manufacturing clusters, which outweighed declines in chemicals and biomedical output. The Monetary Authority of Singapore has said AI-related demand remained firm through the quarter, with any softness in electronics output more likely reflecting capacity constraints in global supply chains than weaker orders. The full sector breakdown with today's release will show which industries drove the upward revision.

A large revision between the advance and final readings is not unusual for Singapore. The advance figure is built largely from July and August data, and last year the third-quarter estimate was also revised up sharply, followed by a forecast upgrade.

The forecasts also carry a warning. Growth of around 6% this year is expected to give way to as little as 2.5% in 2027, as the export boom normalises and comparisons with this year's strong base get tougher. Concentration in AI-related electronics leaves Singapore exposed if technology investment slows, and new US licensing requirements on advanced AI chip shipments to Singapore and four other countries add a further source of uncertainty for the trade hub.

The data will feed into the Monetary Authority of Singapore's next policy review, due no later than January 29. The central bank manages policy through the exchange rate rather than interest rates, and stronger growth gives it more reason to keep its current settings. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Goldman says AI's next test is proving the economics, not the technology
item.description:
Goldman's focus on financing favours companies with strong balance sheets and reliable access to capital, which could widen the valuation gap between cash-rich hyperscalers and highly leveraged AI builders. Its view that agentic AI could push computing demand beyond user growth supports the chip, memory and power supply chain, consistent with its earlier note on AI spending broadening beyond Nvidia. Its expectation that permit and power constraints will shift where capacity is built, not reduce it, points to rising demand for sites with available energy, a theme relevant to utilities and energy markets. For newly listed AI names, the note's emphasis on execution suggests trading will stay sensitive to revenue updates.

---

The big news Monday:

  • Jensen Huang is back in charge. Nvidia moves higher.

---

Goldman's verdict: AI demand looks real, but the industry now has to prove it can pay for the computing that demand requires, and not every player will.

Summary:

  • Goldman Sachs says the AI debate is moving from proving the technology to proving the economics, as focus shifts from training models to running them
  • Citing Anthropic data, it notes around 80% of usage is on the newest models, and customers spending $100,000 or more nearly doubled from Q2 to Q3
  • It says some open-source models are raising prices, which undercuts the idea of an inevitable race to the bottom
  • It says financing is the key question and expects winners to be those with the balance sheets and access to capital to fund computing power
  • It is watching execution, access to infrastructure and buildout limits, which it expects to delay capacity rather than weaken demand

Goldman Sachs says the artificial intelligence debate is shifting from proving the technology to proving the economics, and that the gap between AI winners and laggards may widen as companies are forced to show the spending pays off.

In a note framed around last week's initial public offering of Anthropic, the developer of the Claude AI models, the bank said the IPO comes at an important point in the AI cycle. The industry's focus is moving from training models to running them, a process known as inference, and to putting them to wider use. Anthropic listed on Nasdaq on November 19 after pricing at $83 a share and raising about $81 billion, the largest IPO on record. The shares opened sharply higher but fell about 8.5% the next day as a broad AI sell-off hit technology stocks.

Goldman said there are still returns to being at the frontier of AI. It noted that around 80% of Anthropic's usage is on its newest models, which suggests customers keep choosing greater capability. Models are still improving, both after their initial training and by using more computing power to reason before they answer. The bank added, however, that staying at the frontier requires continued heavy investment.

On competition from open-source models, Goldman said it is watching how competitive advantages evolve. Some open models are raising prices, which challenges the idea of an inevitable race to the bottom. Embedding AI into workflows, data and business processes can raise switching costs, while tailoring products to specific industries offers another potential source of pricing power.

The bank said evidence of real-world demand is building. Citing Anthropic figures, it said the number of customers spending at least $100,000 over the prior 12 months nearly doubled between the second and third quarters, and adoption now extends to more than half of the Fortune 500. Coding remains the largest use case, with cybersecurity growing and healthcare emerging. Agentic AI, which carries out multi-step tasks on its own, could add much more, and because each step consumes computing power, demand for computing could grow faster than the number of users.

The hardest question, in Goldman's view, is financing. Whether the data centres, chips and power behind frontier AI can be funded and built is increasingly a question of capital. The bank expects the winners to be companies with the balance sheet and access to capital to pay for computing power, and the ability to use it profitably. Owning infrastructure and using several types of chips may also reduce dependence on any single supplier.

Goldman said it is watching three things: execution, meaning whether better technology turns into revenue fast enough to justify continued investment; access to computing capacity, sites and cloud partnerships; and buildout limits such as permits, power and data centre restrictions. It expects those limits to delay capacity or shift where it is built rather than weaken demand.

The note's message cuts both ways for investors. Strong adoption data support the case that AI demand is real, but the scale of investment needed means returns are not guaranteed, and the volatile trading in AI stocks since Anthropic's debut shows how quickly sentiment can turn while that question remains open. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Fed's Williams won't rule out back-to-back rate hikes as data drives the path
item.description:
The openness to consecutive hikes adds upside risk to Fed pricing beyond December, with traders more likely to build in a follow-up move in early 2027. That should keep short-dated Treasury yields supported and give the US dollar a firmer floor, especially against currencies whose central banks are moving toward cuts. For equities, Williams set a high bar for market weakness to change his view, which limits hopes that renewed tech volatility would slow the Fed. Energy remains central to his inflation outlook, so any rise in oil prices would add weight to the case for a faster pace of hikes.

---

Earlier:

  • Fed's Williams pins inflation on unusual factors, sees 2027 bringing it lower
  • Williams keeps December Fed hike in play as inflation seen above 2% until 2028

---

Williams' message to reporters was simple: December may only be the start, and only a much deeper slide in market confidence than the recent tech sell-off would make him rethink.

Summary:

  • New York Fed President John Williams says he would not rule out rate hikes at consecutive meetings if needed
  • He says he has no particular timing in mind and has not pencilled in a path, and data will drive decisions
  • He says the Fed will respond if inflation pressures do not ease
  • He is not surprised by market volatility and says tech sector swings have not upended his positive economic outlook
  • He says a big darkening in market sentiment could affect his view of the economy
  • Markets expect a quarter-point hike at the December 8-9 meeting from the 3.75%-4.00% range

New York Federal Reserve President John Williams said on Monday he would not rule out raising interest rates at consecutive meetings if needed, adding a sharper edge to a day of remarks in which he stressed that inflation remains too high.

Speaking to reporters after his speech at the University of Mount Saint Vincent in New York City, Williams said he has no particular timing in mind for further rate increases and has not pencilled in a path for policy. Incoming data will drive what the Fed does, he said, and officials will have to learn along the way. But he was clear that the range of outcomes is wide. "I'm not excluding options," Williams said, adding that he would not rule out moving at back-to-back meetings if that was what was needed. He also said the Fed will respond if inflation pressures do not ease.

That matters for how markets read the December 8-9 meeting. Investors broadly expect a quarter-point increase from the current 3.75% to 4.00% range, with more to come next year. The Fed last raised rates in September, so a December move would follow a pause. Williams' comments suggest a December hike need not be followed by a long wait, and that the pace of tightening could pick up if inflation data disappoint.

Williams also addressed the recent turbulence in stocks. He said he was not surprised by the market volatility and that swings in the tech sector have not upended his positive outlook for the economy. He did leave one caveat: if market sentiment darkened a lot, that could affect his view of the economy.

That caveat sets a high bar. The S&P 500 had slid more than 10% from its October record before Monday's Nvidia-led rebound, and Williams still described the outlook as positive. Read that way, only a deeper and more lasting drop in confidence, one that starts to hit spending and hiring, would be likely to make him rethink the case for tighter policy. Ordinary market swings, even sharp ones, appear unlikely to do so.

His press comments rounded out a consistent message across the day. In his prepared remarks, Williams said inflation is too high, risks are skewed to the upside and the Fed still has work to do, while forecasting inflation at 3.5% at the end of this year and back at the 2% target in 2028. In the question-and-answer session, he struck a more measured tone, describing recent inflation as driven by unusual factors and calling 2027 a year of lower inflation. His remarks to reporters made clear that the measured tone should not be mistaken for a reluctance to act.

The next tests are the economic data releases due before the December meeting. Hot readings would strengthen the case for a faster pace of hikes into early 2027, while softer data would give the Fed room to move more gradually. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: ANZ pulls first RBA rate cut forward to June 2027, sees three cuts by early 2028
item.description:
The bigger story for currency markets is the policy divergence. The RBA is now widely expected to start easing in mid-2027, while the Fed is still on a hiking path, with a December increase broadly expected. A narrowing rate gap between the two would weigh on the Australian dollar against the US dollar over time. Short-dated Australian rates may see limited reaction, because markets had already priced a June cut as more likely than not after the jobs data. The effect is more likely to show up further out on the curve. Any upside surprise in quarterly inflation would test ANZ's call quickly and could prompt a sharp repricing back toward a later start to easing.

---

Yesterday: 

  • Australia flash PMI sinks to 46.1 as private sector shrinks at fastest pace in 5 years

--- After five hikes this year, ANZ thinks the RBA will reverse course by mid-2027, though that depends on inflation cooling faster than the central bank itself expects.

Summary:

  • ANZ has brought its first RBA rate cut forward to June 2027 from November 2027, now ahead of the other big four banks, which expect August 2027
  • It now sees three 25bp cuts: June 2027 (to 4.60%), August 2027 (to 4.35%) and February 2028 (to 4.10%)
  • Head of Australian Economics Adam Boyton says the labour market must weaken further, excess demand must unwind and underlying inflation must moderate over the next six months
  • Boyton says there is already early evidence of all three
  • Unemployment hit a five-year high of 4.9% in October, above the RBA's 4.75% estimate of the jobless rate consistent with stable inflation
  • The RBA hiked for the fifth time this year on November 3, taking the cash rate to 4.85%

ANZ now expects the Reserve Bank of Australia to begin cutting interest rates in June 2027, five months earlier than its previous forecast of November 2027, making it the first of Australia's big four banks to pencil in relief before the second half of next year.

In a research note released on Tuesday, ANZ Head of Australian Economics Adam Boyton set out a new easing path. The bank now sees a 25 basis point cut in June 2027, taking the cash rate from 4.85% to 4.60%, followed by a second cut in August 2027 to 4.35% and a third in February 2028 to 4.10%. Under its previous forecast, ANZ expected only two cuts, in November 2027 and February 2028.

The change comes less than a month after the RBA delivered its fifth rate increase of 2026 on November 3, lifting the cash rate to 4.85%, its highest level since 2008. The other three major banks currently expect the first cut in August 2027.

Boyton said three conditions need to play out over the next six months to justify a cut in the first half of next year: further deterioration in the labour market, an unwinding of excess demand across the economy and a moderation in underlying inflation. He said there is already early evidence pointing toward each of those developments.

The labour market is the most visible of the three. Employment fell sharply for a second straight month in October, pushing the unemployment rate up to 4.9%, a five-year high. That is above 4.75%, the RBA's estimate of the jobless rate consistent with stable inflation, a threshold that matters because it suggests the jobs market is no longer adding to price pressure.

Inflation is the harder test. The RBA's own forecasts, released after its November meeting, show inflation staying above 3% over the coming year and not returning to the top of its 2% to 3% target band until late 2027. For a June cut to happen, underlying price growth would need to slow faster than the central bank currently expects, or the RBA would need to be convinced that a weakening economy will finish the job.

ANZ's call also brings it closer to market pricing rather than ahead of it. After last week's jobs data, markets put the odds of a quarter-point cut at the June 2027 meeting at around 68%, rising to about 90% for August. Because the forecast still implies an extended hold from here, its main effect is on pricing further out along the yield curve rather than on expectations for the next few RBA meetings.

The key risks to the view run in both directions. A rebound in hiring or stubborn services inflation could push cuts back toward the second half of 2027, while a sharper slowdown could bring them forward again. Quarterly inflation and monthly jobs data over the next six months will decide which way the call breaks. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Tokyo gets its first look at the Nvidia whiplash as Asia trades the Huang rebound
item.description:
Asian chip stocks get their first full chance today to respond to Nvidia's reinstatement of Jensen Huang as chief executive, and the setup differs sharply from market to market.

Tokyo is the clearest case. Japanese markets were shut on Monday for a public holiday, so today's session is the first since Friday's AI-led sell-off on Wall Street and Monday's sharp rebound, when the Nasdaq Composite jumped 6.5%. Chip equipment and testing names with close ties to the AI supply chain, such as Advantest and Tokyo Electron, will be the ones to watch.

Seoul has the most ground to recover. The Kospi fell 3.3% to around 4,709 on Monday, with Samsung Electronics down about 3% and SK Hynix down 2.5%, as the region traded Friday's US losses before the Huang news broke. Both memory makers are heavily exposed to AI demand, and US memory chip peer Micron jumped sharply overnight. Goldman Sachs also said in a recent note that demand is outstripping supply in memory, one of the areas where AI investment is increasingly flowing beyond Nvidia.

Taiwan may have less catching up to do. The Taiex rose 2.2% on Monday and TSMC gained 1.5%, so some of the AI optimism was already priced in before the announcement. TSMC's role in advanced packaging, another bottleneck Goldman highlighted, still leaves it well placed if the rebound holds.

Japan's flash PMIs at 0030 GMT (1930 US Eastern) add a macro test early in the session. However, the Nvidia rebound looks likely to drive regional sentiment for much of the day, with traders also weighing whether the narrow, chip-led rally can broaden. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Goldman sees up to $15 trillion for AI infrastructure as spending spreads beyond Nvidia
item.description:
Goldman's framing favours the bottleneck parts of the AI supply chain, particularly memory makers, advanced packaging specialists and power infrastructure, over a single-stock bet on Nvidia. That is relevant for Asian equities, where memory and packaging exposure is concentrated in Korea and Taiwan. The view that neocloud lending now depends on milestones should ease some credit concerns around the sector, although it also implies slower, more conditional build-outs. The power angle ties AI spending to energy and utilities demand, a theme that is likely to keep electricity infrastructure in focus as data centre construction grows.

---

Goldman's message is that the AI build-out is bigger than any one company: even if Nvidia's share shrinks, the trillions keep flowing, just into more hands.

Summary:

  • Goldman Sachs sees $10 trillion to $15 trillion flowing into AI infrastructure over the next six years, with near-term demand intact
  • The note was written before Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang, so some of the leadership risks it weighed have since eased
  • It says "circular financing" concerns need perspective, as Nvidia's commitments are a small fraction of total spending and neocloud lending is getting more disciplined
  • It says demand is outstripping supply in memory, server processors and chipmaking equipment, with spending increasingly reaching areas Nvidia doesn't supply
  • It says any loss of Nvidia market share would change who gets which slice of the pie, not the size of the pie, and that supply constraints limit how fast share can shift

Goldman Sachs believes $10 trillion to $15 trillion could flow into AI infrastructure over the next six years, and argues that a growing share of that spending is reaching companies beyond Nvidia, including memory makers, chip packaging specialists and power suppliers.

The bank's note was written before Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive on Monday, when the company's leadership was still in doubt. That timing matters. Several of the risks it weighed, including uncertainty over Nvidia's product roadmap, have eased with Huang's return. Its central argument does not depend on who runs Nvidia, though: in Goldman's view, near-term demand for AI infrastructure remains intact.

The bank also addressed concerns about so-called circular financing, the worry that Nvidia is funding customers who then use the money to buy its chips. Goldman said those fears need perspective, since Nvidia's outstanding commitments are a small fraction of the total spending it expects. It added that lending to "neoclouds", the newer cloud providers that specialise in renting out AI computing power, is becoming more disciplined. Money is increasingly released only as these firms hit construction milestones, sign up customers and secure sites and power.

On the supply side, Goldman said demand is outstripping supply across memory, server processors and chipmaking equipment. Nvidia sells far more than graphics processors, including networking gear, central processors, complete server systems and the software that ties them together. Even so, the bank noted that investment is increasingly reaching areas Nvidia does not supply, such as memory, advanced packaging, which covers how chips are assembled and connected, and power.

That leads to what may be the note's most useful framing for investors. Goldman said any loss of Nvidia market share would change who gets which slice of the AI pie, not the size of the pie. Supply constraints and long design cycles limit how quickly share can shift, but uncertainty over Nvidia's longer-term roadmap could help rival chip designers and their suppliers. The bank also flagged that if Nvidia's work on open-source models and enterprise tools slowed, closed-model developers could benefit at the expense of software firms that rely on fast open-source progress. Huang's return makes that scenario less likely in the near term.

Monday's market reaction offered a live test of the thesis. When Huang returned, memory makers and other AI suppliers rallied alongside Nvidia, consistent with Goldman's view that the AI spending wave lifts a broad supply chain rather than a single company.

For investors, the takeaway is less about Nvidia's leadership drama than about where AI capital is heading next. If Goldman is right that spending is broadening into memory, packaging and power, the bottlenecks in those areas may matter as much for returns as Nvidia's market share. The main risk to that view is a slowdown in AI investment itself, which would shrink the pie rather than reshuffle it. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Fed's Williams pins inflation on unusual factors, sees 2027 bringing it lower
item.description:
The Q&A softens the tone of Williams' prepared remarks without changing their core message, so pricing for a quarter-point hike on December 9 is unlikely to move much. His focus on unusual factors puts energy back at the centre. Brent is still around $92, well above the roughly $72 seen in late February before the US war with Iran began, so oil remains the main factor in how quickly 2027 delivers the lower inflation he expects. A sustained fall in crude would strengthen the case for a shallower hiking path next year, while fresh supply disruption would push the other way. His caution on hiring matters for the US dollar, since any slowdown in payrolls would weaken the case for further increases beyond December.

---

Williams still wants inflation lower, but his Q&A made clear he sees shocks rather than an overheating economy behind it, which points to steady hikes rather than aggressive ones.

Summary:

  • In Q&A after his speech, New York Fed President John Williams said recent inflation was driven by unusual factors and 2027 will be a year of lower inflation
  • He said the Fed has worked very hard to bring inflation down and has made progress
  • He described the economy as resilient in the face of large challenges, but said the foundations of strong growth face some challenges
  • He said companies want to hire but are being cautious
  • He said the Fed keeps politics out of its policy debates
  • Markets expect a quarter-point hike at the December 8-9 meeting from the 3.75%-4.00% range

New York Federal Reserve President John Williams said on Monday that the recent rise in US inflation has been driven by unusual factors and that he expects 2027 to be a year of lower inflation, striking a more measured tone in a question-and-answer session after his prepared remarks.

Speaking at an event at the University of Mount Saint Vincent in New York City, Williams said the Fed has been working very hard to bring inflation down and had made progress. That did not mark a retreat from his speech, in which he said inflation remains too high, the risks are skewed to the upside and the central bank still has work to do to get back to its 2% goal. His forecasts fit his comment on 2027: he sees inflation ending this year at 3.5%, slowing to just above 2% next year and reaching the target in 2028.

The "unusual factors" line links to the drivers he set out in his prepared text. There he pointed to elevated energy prices, along with tariffs, geopolitical conflicts and the AI investment surge pushing up prices in certain categories of goods, while finding little evidence of those pressures spreading into broader, more persistent inflation. Read together, his remarks suggest he sees the current overshoot as the product of specific shocks rather than an overheating economy. Policymakers who hold that view typically favour a gradual approach to tightening over an aggressive one.

On the economy, Williams said growth has been resilient in the face of many large challenges, though he cautioned that the underpinnings of that strength face some challenges of their own. He also said companies want to hire but are being cautious. That adds a note of caution to his speech, which described the job market as stable and forecast the unemployment rate easing from 4.1% to around 4% next year, alongside growth of 2.75% in both 2026 and 2027.

Williams also stressed that the Fed keeps politics out of its policy debates.

Markets broadly expect the Fed to raise its policy rate by a quarter of a percentage point at its December 8-9 meeting from the current 3.75% to 4.00% range, with further increases expected next year. The Fed last raised rates in September. With that meeting about two weeks away, Williams' comments describe a policymaker still committed to bringing inflation down but alert to softer spots in growth and hiring. That leaves incoming data, and energy prices in particular, to decide how far the Fed goes beyond December. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Nvidia's Huang is back. Monday's rally leaves three big questions unanswered.
item.description:
Asia gets the first real test today of whether the relief extends beyond US chipmakers: Tokyo reopens after a holiday, and Seoul's memory makers sold off before the news broke. In rates, a firmer equity backdrop gives the Fed cover to raise rates in December, which should keep short-dated Treasury yields supported and limit any pullback in the US dollar. Energy shares lagged during the rebound, which suggests the money returning to AI did not spill over into commodity-linked sectors. Nvidia volatility is likely to stay elevated into the December 1 congressional interview, since the stock now prices in a clean resolution of the security questions.

--

  • Nvidia board reinstates Jensen Huang as President and CEO, effective immediately
  • Jensen Huang may be back but the China hawks probably haven't given up
  • Jensen Huang is back in charge. Nvidia moves higher.

--

Nvidia's chips, customers and order book didn't change over the weekend, only the mood did, and a mood that can swing nearly a trillion dollars in a session can swing back just as fast.

Summary:

  • Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, and the stock surged about 31%, while the S&P 500 rose 4.7% and the Nasdaq 6.5%, their best day since April 2025
  • The rebound followed a seven-day slide that left the S&P 500 more than 10% below its October record
  • The board cited senior US government input in judging his return no security risk, but Huang still faces a closed-door House interview on December 1
  • The US tightened AI chip export controls on November 16, requiring licences for shipments to five countries including Singapore and Malaysia
  • New York Fed President John Williams kept a December hike in play on the same day, and the rally weakens any case for the Fed to hesitate
  • The rally was driven by sentiment and was narrow: chip stocks led, software lagged and energy fell

Nvidia's decision to bring back Jensen Huang as chief executive gave Wall Street its best session since April 2025 on Monday, but the rally answered only one question: who runs the world's most important AI chipmaker. Three other issues that could matter more for markets in the coming weeks remain open. They are the unresolved security questions around Huang, a Federal Reserve that is still leaning towards higher rates, and how much of the US stock market now rides on confidence in a single company.

The S&P 500 jumped 4.7% to about 7,237 and the Nasdaq Composite surged 6.5%, while the Dow added around 1,450 points. Nvidia shares soared about 31% to close near $165. The rebound followed a seven-day slide that had left the S&P 500 more than 10% below its October 6 record, capped by a 5.3% drop in the Nasdaq on Friday as worries over AI valuations and spending collided with Nvidia's leadership crisis.

1. The security questions have not gone away

Huang resigned on November 12 after reports of affairs, including one with a former Megaspeed executive whom US officials suspect of spying for China. Beijing denies she is a spy. Nvidia's board had already opened an independent investigation on November 8 into reports that Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort. In reinstating him, the board said it was satisfied with his candour and cited input from senior levels of the US government in concluding that his return poses no national security risk.

That is an assurance, not a published finding, and Washington's scrutiny has not stopped. Huang is due to face a closed-door interview with three House committees on December 1, according to reports. Separately, the Commerce Department on November 16 tightened controls on advanced AI chips, requiring licences for shipments to Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and Brazil because of the risk of diversion to China. Any damaging disclosure from Capitol Hill would land on a stock that has just repriced on the assumption the matter is closed.

2. The Fed is still on a hiking path

On the same day, New York Fed President John Williams said inflation remains too high and the Fed still has work to do, with risks skewed to the upside. Markets broadly expect a quarter-point increase at the December 8-9 meeting from the current 3.75% to 4.00% range. Some observers had wondered whether last week's equity losses might make the Fed hesitate. A 4.7% rally in the S&P 500 removes that argument, and higher rates tend to weigh hardest on richly valued growth stocks, the same AI names that led Monday's rebound.

3. One company is carrying the market's mood

The most striking feature of Monday was that nothing about Nvidia's chips, customers or order book changed over the weekend. What changed was confidence. Before the announcement, one wealth strategist described a "crisis of confidence" across the AI trade, and Nvidia sits at the centre of that ecosystem as supplier, partner and bellwether. When its leadership looked uncertain, doubts spread to the whole AI buildout. When Huang returned, investors rushed back into memory makers, rival chip designers and the hyperscalers, with AMD up around 6% and Alphabet and Meta each gaining more than 5%.

That makes the rebound as much a sentiment event as a valuation call, and it was narrow. Chip stocks surged around 13% at one point, software gained only about 4%, and energy and real estate actually fell. The relief was concentrated in AI hardware, not spread across the market. For anyone holding an S&P 500 or Nasdaq index fund, it is also a reminder that a large slice of their portfolio carries key-person risk tied to one executive, whether they chose that exposure or not.

What to watch

Confidence that returns in a single session can leave just as quickly. The next tests are the December 1 congressional interview, the Fed's December 8-9 decision, and whether Monday's rally broadens beyond chipmakers. If Nvidia can hold most of its gains through those events, the rebound will look like a genuine reset rather than a one-day burst of relief. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Jensen Huang is back in charge. Nvidia moves higher.
item.description:
The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite had their best day since April 9, 2025, as buyers returned to beaten-down AI and chip stocks. Nvidia led the rebound, jumping $39.52 to $165.05 after its board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO. The Nasdaq 100 gained 6.86%, the biggest move among the major US indices, while the Dow added more than 1,448 points.

The buying spread well beyond Nvidia. The Russell 2000 rose 3.40%, 26 of the 30 Dow stocks advanced, and S&P 500 gainers outnumbered decliners 406 to 79. Both Nasdaq indices recovered all of Friday’s losses, and the S&P 500 snapped a seven-session losing streak. The four major indices with reported intraday ranges stayed positive throughout the session and each held more than 84% of its peak point gain into the close. images.investinglive.com

Crude oil moved the other way. WTI settled down $3.24, or 3.88%, at $80.17 as Middle East supply increased and a Libyan pipeline reopened. If the decline sticks, it could ease some of the pressure on fuel costs and headline inflation. The next US data point is consumer confidence Tuesday at 10 a.m. ET. The NYSE is closed Thursday for Thanksgiving and closes at 1 p.m. ET on Friday.

US closing levels

  • Dow Industrial Average +1,448.12 points (+3.01%) to 49,599.95
  • S&P 500 +326.78 points (+4.73%) to 7,237.17
  • Nasdaq Composite +1,471.82 points (+6.51%) to 24,089.56
  • Russell 2000 +87.87 points (+3.40%) to 2,669.66
  • Nasdaq 100 +1,717.11 points (+6.86%) to 26,746.10

The Dow was up 881.48 points at its low and 1,658.43 points at its high. The Nasdaq 100 was up 1,357.43 points at its low and 1,989.89 points at its high, briefly trading above 27,000 before closing back below it.

S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite levels to watch

S&P 500. The index closed at 7,237.17 after trading as much as 385.77 points higher. The first upside target is Monday’s high at 7,296.16, just below 7,300. Buyers need to get above that area and stay above it to extend the rebound. On the downside, Monday’s low at 7,152.86 gives buyers a level to lean against on a deeper pullback. A move below that low that sticks would give sellers more control and put Friday’s close at 6,910.39 back in view.

Nasdaq Composite. The index reached 24,353.65, up 1,735.91 points at the high, before closing at 24,089.56. The first test for buyers is whether they can hold above 24,000 on a pullback. If they do, Monday’s high is the next target. A sustained move below 24,000 would shift attention to the session low at 23,794.96. Buyers looking to lean against that low have a defined risk level. If it gives way and the price stays below it, Friday’s close at 22,617.74 comes back into view.

AI and chip stocks lead. All seven megacaps gain.

  • AI infrastructure and connectivity: Astera Labs +23.16%, Credo Technology +22.63%, CoreWeave +22.32%, Nebius +20.28%, and Lumentum +18.20%.
  • Semiconductors: Nvidia +31.48%, Micron +19.04%, Marvell +18.37%, Intel +16.34%, and Arm +16.08%. The VanEck Semiconductor ETF gained 15.03%.
  • The rest of the Magnificent Seven: Tesla +11.46%, Meta +6.55%, Alphabet +6.34%, Amazon +3.47%, Apple +1.90%, and Microsoft +1.65%.

European stocks also closed higher. Germany’s DAX led the group, up 2.16%, followed by Spain’s IBEX 35 at +1.63%, France’s CAC 40 at +1.48%, the UK’s FTSE 100 at +1.30%, and Italy’s FTSE MIB at +0.65%.

Trading lesson. See what buyers defend on the pullback.

Big up days can leave traders with wide risk. At Monday’s close, the Nasdaq Composite was nearly 295 points above its session low. If that low is the level you’re leaning against, that’s the distance you have to account for before entering. A pullback that holds near 24,000 could give buyers a closer level to lean against. If the price goes through that level and stays below it, the market is telling you that buyers need to prove themselves again at the next level.

item.title: Economic and event calendar in Asia Tuesday, November 24, 2026: Singapore and Japan
item.description:
Singapore Q3 GDP: 0000 GMT / 1900 US Eastern

Singapore starts the Asian data day with third-quarter GDP. Economists expect growth of 1.3% quarter on quarter, up from 1.1% in the previous reading. On a year-on-year basis, they expect 5.6% against 5.4% before.

If the figures land on forecast, they will confirm that the city-state's economy gained speed through the third quarter, at a strong annual pace for a mature, trade-dependent economy. Singapore is often read as a bellwether for regional trade, so a strong print would point to steady demand across Asia's export supply chains. That matters for the region's manufacturing story heading into the end of the year.

A beat on the year-on-year number would add to the picture of resilient regional activity. A miss would raise questions about how long that momentum can last. Watch also for any change to official full-year growth expectations, which can move the Singapore dollar and local rates. 

The data will also feed into the Monetary Authority of Singapore's next policy review. MAS has scheduled its January 2027 statement for release no later than 29 January, after its last decision on 14 October. Unlike most central banks, MAS does not set an interest rate. It runs monetary policy through the exchange rate, adjusting the slope, width and centre of the Singapore dollar nominal effective exchange rate (S$NEER) policy band, and since 2024 it has issued decisions four times a year, in January, April, July and October. A stronger-than-expected GDP print would give policymakers more reason to keep their current settings in January.

Japan flash PMIs (November): 0030 GMT / 1930 US Eastern

Half an hour later, Jibun Bank's preliminary November PMIs give the first look at how Japanese businesses fared this month. The manufacturing reading is expected at 53.5, up from 53.3. That would mean another month of solid expansion, well above the 50 line that separates growth from contraction.

There is no consensus for services, which read 51.7 last time, so any move either way could stand out more. A firm services number would show domestic demand is holding up alongside the factory sector.

Traders should look past the headline figures to the price components. Input costs and selling prices will show whether firms are still passing higher costs on to customers, including energy costs. That is a key consideration for the Bank of Japan's policy outlook and for the yen. Strong activity and firm price gauges would support the case for tighter policy in Japan.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

  • USD leads, EUR lags
  • S&P 500 up 4.8%
  • Nasdaq up 6.5%
  • WTI crude oil  down $3.34 to $80.10

Two weeks of exile and a massive market rout was enough to prompt a major re-think on the importance of Jensen Huang. We learned today that Nvidia's board met Sunday night to talk about re-instating Huang and President Trump was on the call to advocate for his return. We also found out that US officials cleared him in terms of national security in a move that also likely came from the top.

The reaction was unambiguous with share of Nvidia jumping 24% intially and finishing 31% higher. Much of Friday's pain was also undone in broader markets, and often more. The one-day gains were the largest since April 8, 2025, when Trump TACO'd on Liberation Day tariffs.

Still, there was some level of anxiety in markets. Initially, there was some selling at the open, raising fears of a reversal. Later, even as stocks hit new highs, the fears lingered. Many were waiting to see if there would be a strong or weak finish but ultimately it was sidways. That's certainly a win for bulls but it's tough to signal the 'all clear' from here given the dismal price action from last week. Huang's return doesn't answer all the questions about AI spending and financing so we will get back to debating that in short order.

Elsewhere, oil prices fell again with WTI touching below $80 for the first time since late August. That comes with Iran making more noise about intolerance to the 'no war, no peace' status quo. The talk about running the US blockade continues while ships transiting Hormuz continue to be damaged and some in Congress angle to restrain US offensive authorization.
